newsitem.title: USA: AT&T, MCI cut U.S. long distance phone rates.
newsitem.headline: AT&T, MCI cut U.S. long distance phone rates.

text.p: AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp. said Monday they will cut their basic rates for domestic long-distance calls by 5 percent during daytime and evening hours and 15 percent during night and weekend hours.

The move is expected to be followed by other long-distance providers as they realise at least $1.7 billion in estimated annual industry savings from paying lower access fees for completing calls on Baby Bell companies' local networks.
The access charge reductions, which were ordered by the Federal Communications Commission in May, take effect Tuesday.

AT&T initiated the rate cuts, which will be effective July 15. MCI matched the reductions but will implement them earlier, on Wednesday. The cuts apply only to customers who are not enrolled in a calling plan.
AT&T, which controls more than half the long-distance market, said it is passing on all its savings, which analysts estimate at $900 million to $930 million a year.
But Bell Atlantic Corp. responded soon after AT&T's announcement that it filed a complaint with the FCC alleging the No. 1 long-distance carrier was pocketing some of the savings.
"We're suspicious, and we think AT&T customers should be suspicious, particularly basic rate payers," said Bell Atlantic spokeswoman Shannon Fioravanti.
AT&T denied Bell Atlantic's charges.
AT&T, based in Basking Ridge, N.J., has committed in writing to the FCC that it would pass on all its access fee savings, but its competitors so far have not.
MCI said in a statement it was delivering on its promise to reduce long-distance phone rates by passing through interstate access charge savings.
MCI said that while the FCC ordered permanent reductions in interstate access charges totalling $1.7 billion, the local phone monopolies have filed reductions of only $1.5 billion.

"These companies are shortchanging America's consumers by $200 million," MCI said. "The FCC should deliver on its promise by forcing the (local phone companies) to obey the law and deliver up the savings to American consumers and businesses. It's only the local phone monopolies that are standing between consumers and even lower long-distance prices."
Analysts said they expect other long-distance carriers to cut basic rates as well.
"Other carriers will follow through, but they haven't been as specific as AT&T in saying how or when," said Bob Wilkes, an analyst with Brown Brothers Harriman.
"Typically, the others do follow, although not in lock step" said Frank Governali, a telecommunications analyst with CS First Boston Corp.
Sprint Corp. spokeswoman Robin Pence said the company had not determined its share of the savings from the access charge cuts, or specifically what to do.
"If our costs go down, we will pass on the savings to our customers as we have in the past," Pence said.
"In a competitive environment like this, no one can really afford to hang onto a cost savings and not pass it on to customers," said AT&T spokesman Jim McGann.
Under AT&T's current basic schedule, a 15-minute coast-to-coast direct-dialed call costs $4.65 during daytime hours, $2.85 during evening hours, and $2.40 during night/weekend hours.
Beginning July 15, the same call will cost $4.35, $2.70 and $1.95, respectively.
McGann would not elaborate on benefits to customers on other rate plans. "Those details will be part of marketing promotions that we're not revealing for now."
AT&T's stock fell 75 cents to $35.06 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange. MCI fell 97 cents to $38.28 on Nasdaq.
